clinicalPearls: Glomerular disease is grouped into six clinical syndromes that overlap and are not mutually exclusive: acute nephritic, pulmonary-renal, nephrotic, basement membrane, glomerular-vascular, and infectious disease-associated (Harrison 22e p.2414-2416).

Nephritic syndrome = inflammatory pattern: hematuria with red blood cell casts, dysmorphic red cells, pyuria, hypertension, fluid retention, only mild-to-moderate (1-2 g/24 h) proteinuria, and a falling GFR (Harrison 22e p.2414, 2416).

Nephrotic syndrome = heavy proteinuria (>3.0-3.5 g/24 h) with hypoalbuminemia, hypercholesterolemia, edema/anasarca, hypertension, and only minimal/microscopic hematuria; isolated heavy proteinuria without these features is termed nephrotic-range proteinuria (Harrison 22e p.2414, 2420).
Red blood cell casts or dysmorphic red cells in the sediment make glomerulonephritis likely; as few as 3-5 red cells in spun first-morning urine is suspicious (Harrison 22e p.2414).
Gross hematuria is rare in glomerular disease except in IgA nephropathy and sickle cell disease; most glomerular hematuria is asymptomatic and microscopic (Harrison 22e p.2414).

Kidney biopsy is the key diagnostic step in most glomerulonephritis; it identifies the lesion and often directs treatment, but is reserved for clinically stable patients with adequate clotting who can receive therapy (Harrison 22e p.2416-2417).

Minimal change disease (MCD) causes 70-90% of childhood nephrotic syndrome but only 10-15% in adults; light microscopy is normal, immunofluorescence negative (or scant mesangial IgM), and electron microscopy shows foot-process effacement; childhood proteinuria is selective (mostly albumin) (Harrison 22e p.2420-2421).

FSGS is the most common cause of primary glomerular disease leading to ESKD in the US; lesions are focal and segmental and concentrated at the corticomedullary junction, so a superficial biopsy can miss them and be misread as MCD (Harrison 22e p.2421-2422).

Membranous glomerulonephritis (MGN) accounts for ~25% of adult nephrotic syndrome; 70-80% of primary cases have circulating IgG4 anti-PLA2R antibodies, and biopsy may no longer be required when anti-PLA2R is positive with normal creatinine and no secondary cause (Harrison 22e p.2422-2423).

IgA nephropathy is defined by dominant/codominant mesangial IgA deposits and is one of the most common glomerulonephritides worldwide; the two classic presentations are persistent asymptomatic microscopic hematuria and recurrent gross hematuria during/just after an upper respiratory infection (synpharyngitic) (Harrison 22e p.2419).

Membranoproliferative GN (MPGN) is now viewed as a pattern of injury (mesangial/subendothelial immune complexes, complement, or monoclonal deposits) producing GBM double contours ('tram-tracking'), rather than a single disease; classify by underlying immune-complex, complement, or monoclonal cause (Harrison 22e p.2420-2421).

C3 glomerulopathy (dense deposit disease and C3 glomerulonephritis) shows sole/dominant glomerular C3 with little or no immunoglobulin and is driven by alternative-complement-pathway dysregulation (e.g., CFHR mutations, C3 nephritic factor) (Harrison 22e p.2420).

RPGN is the clinical picture of acute nephritis with serum creatinine rising over days; crescentic glomerulonephritis is its pathologic equivalent and warrants urgent biopsy and treatment (Harrison 22e p.2414, 2419).
When RPGN presents with lung hemorrhage it is a pulmonary-renal syndrome; consider anti-GBM/Goodpasture disease, ANCA small-vessel vasculitis, lupus, and cryoglobulinemia (Harrison 22e p.2414, 2418).

ANCA small-vessel vasculitis (GPA, MPA, EGPA, renal-limited) causes a pauci-immune (little/no immune-complex deposition) segmental necrotizing/crescentic glomerulonephritis; anti-PR3 is more common in GPA and anti-MPO in MPA/EGPA (Harrison 22e p.2419-2420).

Anti-GBM disease targets the alpha3 NC1 domain of type IV collagen; biopsy shows linear IgG staining along the GBM (versus the granular 'lumpy-bumpy' deposits of immune-complex disease); 10-15% also have anti-MPO ANCA (Harrison 22e p.2418-2419).

Poststreptococcal GN classically shows subepithelial 'humps' on electron microscopy, low C3/CH50 with normal C4 in the first week, and a positive streptozyme test; it rarely requires biopsy and has a good prognosis in children (Harrison 22e p.2417-2418).

Lupus nephritis is classified ISN/RPS class I-VI; proliferative class III/IV lesions (and class IV with crescents) carry the worst prognosis, while mesangial class I/II need little therapy and class V is a membranous pattern (Harrison 22e p.2418).

Kidney failure in glomerulonephritis correlates histologically with the degree of tubulointerstitial nephritis and interstitial fibrosis rather than with the specific glomerular lesion; interstitial fibrosis is an ominous sign of irreversibility (Harrison 22e p.2413-2414, 2416).

On biopsy, <50% glomerular involvement is focal and >50% diffuse; injury within a tuft is segmental (part) or global (most); endocapillary proliferation is within the tuft and extracapillary proliferation (crescents) extends into Bowman's space (Harrison 22e p.2417).
harrison.pathophysiology: Each kidney holds ~0.9 million glomerular tufts whose fenestrated endothelium, GBM, and podocyte foot processes with slit-pore membranes form a size- and charge-selective filtration barrier; glomerular injury allows gram quantities of protein (mainly albumin) to escape (Harrison 22e p.2411-2412). Disease arises through genetic mutations (e.g., NPHS1/nephrin, NPHS2/podocin, TRPC6, APOL1 risk variants for FSGS; type IV collagen alpha3/4/5 in Alport's; complement-pathway/CFHR mutations in MPGN and C3 glomerulopathy/aHUS), infection, toxins, autoimmunity, hypertension/atherosclerosis, thrombosis/emboli, and diabetes; many cases remain idiopathic (Harrison 22e p.2411-2412). Inflammation of glomerular capillaries (glomerulonephritis) is typically immune-mediated: preformed circulating immune complexes deposit on the subendothelial side or mesangium, while in-situ formation produces subepithelial deposits; anti-GBM antibodies bind linearly to the GBM. Deposits and Toll-like receptor activation recruit neutrophils, macrophages, and T cells, activate complement to C5-9 membrane-attack complexes, and release proteases and oxidants that damage the mesangium, capillaries, and GBM and efface podocytes; early CD4/CD8 T-cell activation is important. Depending on antigen location and host genetics, injury produces endocapillary or extracapillary (crescentic) proliferation. Progression to chronic kidney failure tracks with downstream tubulointerstitial nephritis and fibrosis, driven by proteinuria-laden filtrate, inflammatory mediators carried from inflamed glomeruli, and fibroblast/myofibroblast expansion (TGF-beta, FGF-2, HIF-1alpha, PDGF) laying down collagen (Harrison 22e p.2412-2414).
additionalDifferentials: Acute nephritic syndrome: poststreptococcal GN, subacute bacterial endocarditis-associated GN, lupus nephritis, anti-GBM disease, IgA nephropathy, ANCA small-vessel vasculitis (GPA, MPA, EGPA), IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schonlein purpura), cryoglobulinemia, MPGN, C3 glomerulopathy, mesangioproliferative GN (Harrison 22e p.2414-2415).

Nephrotic syndrome: minimal change disease, FSGS, membranous glomerulonephritis, diabetic nephropathy, AL/AA amyloidosis, light-chain deposition disease, fibrillary-immunotactoid disease, Fabry's disease (Harrison 22e p.2415).
Pulmonary-renal syndromes: Goodpasture's/anti-GBM disease, ANCA vasculitis, IgA vasculitis, cryoglobulinemia (Harrison 22e p.2414-2415).
Basement membrane syndromes: anti-GBM disease, Alport's syndrome, thin basement membrane disease, nail-patella syndrome (Harrison 22e p.2415).
Glomerular vascular syndromes: atherosclerotic and hypertensive nephropathy, cholesterol emboli, sickle cell disease, thrombotic microangiopathies, antiphospholipid syndrome (Harrison 22e p.2415).

Microscopic hematuria with minimal proteinuria can also reflect non-glomerular causes: urinary tract malignancy (especially older men), BPH, interstitial nephritis, papillary necrosis, hypercalciuria, kidney stones, cystic kidney disease, or renal vascular injury (Harrison 22e p.2414).
infectionMimics: Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis after nephritogenic streptococcal pharyngitis (1-3 weeks) or skin infection (2-6 weeks) (Harrison 22e p.2417-2418).

Subacute bacterial endocarditis-associated and other persistent-infection (shunt, abscess, infected prosthesis; often Staphylococcus) glomerulonephritis, which can mimic or coexist with ANCA vasculitis (Harrison 22e p.2417).

Hepatitis B and C (membranous, MPGN, cryoglobulinemic patterns), HIV-associated nephropathy (collapsing FSGS), syphilis, leprosy, malaria, and schistosomiasis - globally, malaria and schistosomiasis may be the most common causes of glomerulonephritis (Harrison 22e p.2416, 2459).
IgA-dominant Staphylococcus-associated infectious glomerulonephritis can mimic primary IgA nephropathy (Harrison 22e p.2419).
nonInfectiousMimics: Diabetic nephropathy and amyloidosis both thicken the GBM and can mimic membranous nephropathy on light microscopy (Harrison 22e p.2422-2423).

Secondary FSGS (adaptive hyperfiltration/obesity, reflux, hypertension, drugs such as heroin/interferon/bisphosphonates, viruses) and genetic/familial podocytopathies must be excluded before diagnosing primary FSGS, as immunosuppression is not indicated in secondary/genetic forms (Harrison 22e p.2421-2422).
Secondary membranous nephropathy from malignancy (breast, lung, colon), infection, lupus or other autoimmune disease, IgG4 disease, or drugs (gold, penicillamine, NSAIDs) (Harrison 22e p.2422).
Membranous lupus nephritis (subendothelial deposits/tubuloreticular inclusions) may precede extrarenal lupus and mimic primary MGN (Harrison 22e p.2423).
C3 glomerulopathy can be morphologically indistinguishable from resolving postinfectious glomerulonephritis (Harrison 22e p.2420).
Mesangioproliferative pattern is shared by IgA nephropathy, P. falciparum malaria, resolving postinfectious GN, and lupus class II (Harrison 22e p.2421).
additionalInvestigations: Urinalysis with microscopy for dysmorphic red cells, red blood cell casts, pyuria; quantify proteinuria by spot urine albumin/creatinine ratio (UACR >30 mg/g abnormal) or 24-h collection; distinguish selective (albumin-predominant, childhood MCD) from nonselective proteinuria (Harrison 22e p.2414).

Serologies: ASO/anti-DNase/antihyaluronidase and streptozyme; ANA and anti-dsDNA; complement C3 and C4 (low C3 with normal C4 in poststreptococcal GN and C3 glomerulopathy; hypocomplementemia in active lupus nephritis); ANCA (anti-PR3, anti-MPO); anti-GBM antibody to the alpha3 NC1 domain specifically; cryoglobulins and rheumatoid factor; antiphospholipid antibodies; HIV and hepatitis B/C serologies (Harrison 22e p.2416).
Target-antigen antibodies in nephrotic disease: anti-PLA2R and anti-THSD7A (membranous nephropathy); DNAJB9 (fibrillary GN) (Harrison 22e p.2416-2417, 2422-2423).
Kidney ultrasound to assess kidney size (small kidneys suggest chronicity) and exclude obstruction (Harrison 22e p.2416).

Kidney biopsy with light microscopy (H&E, PAS, Jones silver, Congo red, Masson trichrome), immunofluorescence (IgG/IgM/IgA, C3/C4, PLA2R/THSD7A/DNAJB9), and electron microscopy to localize deposits and assess the GBM (Harrison 22e p.2416-2417).
C3 nephritic factor, factor H, soluble C5b-9, paraprotein screening, and CFHR genetic testing (with family screening) when C3 glomerulopathy is suspected (Harrison 22e p.2420).
redFlags: RPGN / crescentic glomerulonephritis - serum creatinine rising over days is a nephrologic emergency requiring urgent biopsy and immunosuppression (Harrison 22e p.2414, 2419).

Pulmonary-renal syndrome (glomerulonephritis with lung hemorrhage/hemoptysis and falling hemoglobin) - consider anti-GBM/Goodpasture, ANCA vasculitis, lupus, cryoglobulinemia; lung hemorrhage responds to plasmapheresis (Harrison 22e p.2414, 2418-2419).
Anti-GBM disease with oliguria, serum creatinine >5-6 mg/dL, need for acute dialysis, or >50% crescents on biopsy - markers of a poor prognosis requiring prompt treatment (Harrison 22e p.2419).
ANCA small-vessel vasculitis - high mortality without treatment; virtually all patients need urgent induction therapy (Harrison 22e p.2419).
Malignant hypertension can rapidly complicate glomerulosclerosis with fibrinoid arteriolar necrosis, thrombotic microangiopathy, and acute kidney failure (Harrison 22e p.2412).
Nephrotic syndrome is a hypercoagulable state - membranous nephropathy carries the highest risk of renal vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, and deep-vein thrombosis (Harrison 22e p.2423).
harrison.prognosis: Prognosis is lesion-specific and tracks with the degree of tubulointerstitial fibrosis. Poststreptococcal GN resolves in most children within 3-6 weeks with rare progression to ESKD, but is worse in the elderly (up to 60% azotemia) (Harrison 22e p.2418). Minimal change disease responds to steroids in 90-95% of children and 80-90% of adults though relapse is common (70-75% of children) (Harrison 22e p.2421). Primary FSGS with nephrotic-range proteinuria reaches ESKD in ~50% by 10 years and rarely remits spontaneously, but treatment-induced remission improves outcome (Harrison 22e p.2421-2422). In membranous nephropathy roughly one-third remit spontaneously, one-third have relapsing nephrotic syndrome with preserved function, and one-third progress to kidney failure or die of complications (Harrison 22e p.2423). IgA nephropathy progresses to ESKD in only 25-30% over 20-25 years; persistent proteinuria >=6 months is the strongest adverse predictor (Harrison 22e p.2419). Dense deposit disease progresses to ESKD in ~50%. Untreated RPGN/crescentic disease and ANCA vasculitis carry high mortality, but ANCA vasculitis achieves remission in 75-90% with treatment (relapse 25-50%) (Harrison 22e p.2419-2420).
pitfalls: A superficial kidney biopsy that fails to sample deeper corticomedullary glomeruli can miss the focal/segmental lesions of FSGS and be misdiagnosed as minimal change disease - suspect FSGS in steroid-resistant 'MCD' (Harrison 22e p.2421-2422).

Test serum specifically against the alpha3 NC1 domain of collagen IV: non-nephritic anti-alpha1 NC1 antibodies in paraneoplastic syndromes cannot be distinguished by assays using whole basement-membrane fragments (Harrison 22e p.2419).
ANCA-associated vasculitis can accompany or be confused with subacute bacterial endocarditis-associated GN; it must be ruled out because the treatments differ (Harrison 22e p.2417).
There is no role for immunosuppression in poststreptococcal GN even when crescents are present, nor in secondary or genetic FSGS (Harrison 22e p.2418, 2422).

Glomerular hematuria is usually microscopic and asymptomatic, so the diagnosis is often delayed; isolated microscopic hematuria in older men still requires exclusion of urinary tract malignancy (Harrison 22e p.2414).

Nephrotic-range proteinuria without edema or hypoalbuminemia is not necessarily full nephrotic syndrome, and transient/orthostatic proteinuria (fever, exercise, obesity, CHF, upright posture) must be distinguished from sustained pathologic proteinuria (Harrison 22e p.2414, 2420).
harrison.severityClassification: Glomerular disease is organized into six clinical syndromes (acute nephritic, pulmonary-renal, nephrotic, basement membrane, glomerular-vascular, infectious disease-associated) graded semiquantitatively by proteinuria, hematuria, and vascular injury (Table 326-2, Harrison 22e p.2414-2416). Biopsy descriptors: focal (<50% of glomeruli) vs diffuse (>50%); segmental (part of a tuft) vs global; endocapillary vs extracapillary (crescentic) proliferation (Harrison 22e p.2417). Lupus nephritis uses the ISN/RPS class I-VI scheme (I minimal mesangial, II mesangial proliferative, III focal, IV diffuse, V membranous, VI sclerotic) (Table 326-3, Harrison 22e p.2418). IgA nephropathy uses the Oxford MEST-C score (mesangial/endocapillary hypercellularity, segmental sclerosis, tubular fibrosis, crescents) (Harrison 22e p.2419). Albuminuria is staged normal (8-10 mg/24 h), microalbuminuria (30-300 mg/24 h), and frank proteinuria (>300 mg/24 h) (Table 326-1, Harrison 22e p.2414).
management: Direct disease-specific immunosuppression by biopsy-proven lesion, using corticosteroids with agents such as cyclophosphamide, rituximab, calcineurin inhibitors or mycophenolate for immune-mediated glomerulonephritis
Renin-angiotensin blockade with an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker to reduce proteinuria and control blood pressure, the cornerstone of non-immunological management
Manage oedema and volume overload with dietary salt restriction and diuretics, and treat nephrotic hyperlipidaemia with a statin
Reduce thrombotic risk with anticoagulation in severe nephrotic states, and treat the underlying trigger such as infection, lupus or vasculitis
Urgent immunosuppression with plasma exchange for rapidly progressive crescentic disease such as anti-GBM or ANCA-associated glomerulonephritis
Monitor renal function, proteinuria and blood pressure, avoid nephrotoxins, and provide immunisation appropriate to immunosuppression
Refer to nephrology for kidney biopsy to guide therapy, and plan renal replacement therapy or transplantation for progression to established kidney failure
